summary: The bot builds one OpenAI client, and all four of its chat completions calls (chat, plugin follow-up, vision, history summary) now reach Router through the vendored runtime, each labelled with the feature it serves. One of them had to change shape first: the plugin result was recorded without the call that produced it, which Chat Completions tolerates and the Responses API rejects. Image generation, text-to-speech and Whisper stay on OpenAI because Router has no endpoint for them, and the runtime leaves them untouched. Because every call here blocks a Telegram user, router.policy.json pins the standard service tier on Router-bound requests.
reviewed: Model per task, the retry on rate limits, prompt caching, request timeouts and spend labels; summarising an over-long history with the chat model was the one clear waste, and a cheaper model for it is the only change proposed.

items.title: Route the bot's chat calls through Router
items.summary: The single OpenAI client in OpenAIHelper sends the chat, streamed chat, vision and summary requests to Router, each labelled with the feature it serves.
items.gains: Four of the seven LLM calls on Router behind one key, with spend recorded per feature (chat, vision, plugin_call, summary) instead of per file and function
items.loses: Nothing the bot can do. An operator running a Flex-eligible model (gpt-5*, gpt-6*) gives up Router's Flex discount, measured at -50% on gpt-5.4-mini, because the standard tier is pinned for calls a Telegram user waits on; the default gpt-4o has no Flex tier, so nothing changes for it.
items.price: no change: gpt-4o is $2.50/$10 per 1M tokens in Router's catalog, as on OpenAI
items.why: Every request goes through the one client built in OpenAIHelper.__init__, so the runtime under it covers all of them, and the app is untouched until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set. Each call site already knows its job, so it sends that name in x-router-migrate-feature rather than leaving the runtime to derive one from the call stack. Every call in this bot is in a Telegram user's request path, including the summary, which runs inline before the user's answer: router.policy.json therefore sets service_tier "default" for all of them, because Router's account default is cost-efficient routing and one Flex call has been measured at 61 s. Configurations the runtime deliberately keeps on OpenAI, unchanged, so nothing is lost: N_CHOICES>1, a non-zero PRESENCE_PENALTY, models outside Router's catalog (gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4, gpt-4-turbo, o1, chatgpt-4o-latest) and a custom OPENAI_BASE_URL.

evidence.detail: check --run --live over a driver that calls each path with minimal inputs: 5 requests, all 200 /v1/responses model=gpt-4o provider=openai, features chat (buffered and streamed), summary, vision, plugin_call; the run logged 'router-migrate policy 724f9b5c', so the standard tier was applied
check --run on the same driver: 5 of 5 Router requests valid; generate_image, generate_speech and transcribe were kept on the provider by the runtime, as intended
the repo's suite (compileall bot plus importing openai_helper, plugin_manager, telegram_bot, main) with Router on: 5 passed, as on the base commit
router-migrate levers gpt-4o: in $2.50, out $10.00 per 1M tokens, flex no, served on responses and messages

items.title: Pair a plugin result with the call that made it
items.summary: The chat history now holds the model's function call ahead of its result, so the plugin follow-up request is one Router can serve.
items.gains: The plugin follow-up call, and every later turn of a conversation that used a plugin, are served on Router instead of being rejected with 400
items.loses: The model now sees the call it made, not only the bare result, so answers after a plugin call can differ; the history holds one extra message per plugin call, which counts towards MAX_HISTORY_SIZE and the token total shown by SHOW_USAGE
items.why: __handle_function_call appended the plugin result to the history on its own, with no record of the call that produced it. Chat Completions tolerates that; on the Responses API the result becomes a function_call_output whose call_id names no call in the same input, and Router answers 400 'No tool call found for function call output with call_id call_legacy' (the simulator showed exactly that before this change). Because the orphan result stays in the history, it would have broken not just the follow-up but every later turn of that conversation. Recording the assistant's function_call first is the documented shape of the functions API, so the provider path is also better formed; __count_tokens was extended to handle that message (content None plus a function_call dict).

evidence.detail: check --run on the plugin path: INVALID before the change ('No tool call found for function call output with call_id call_legacy'), valid after; 5 of 5 Router requests valid
check --run --live: 200 /v1/responses model=gpt-4o feature=plugin_call provider=openai, and the model went on to call a second plugin from the result
new tests/test_function_call_history.py (PYTHONPATH=bot python -m unittest discover -s tests): 3 passed, covering the history order, the matching call ids after translation, and the token count
the repo's suite with Router on: 5 passed, as on the base commit

items.title: Image generation stays on OpenAI
items.summary: The /image command keeps calling OpenAI's images endpoint.
items.why: Router serves no images endpoint (/v1/images/generations returns 404), so there is nowhere to send this request. The runtime recognises image requests and leaves them on the provider, which is why the OPENAI_API_KEY has to stay configured.

evidence.detail: check --run: the request is reported as 'provider (runtime kept it): model=dall-e-2', never offered to Router

items.title: Voice in and out stay on OpenAI
items.summary: Text-to-speech and Whisper transcription keep calling OpenAI's audio endpoints.
items.why: Router has no audio endpoints at all, so neither speech synthesis nor transcription can move; audio input on Responses is refused as well. The runtime keeps both requests on OpenAI untouched.

evidence.detail: check --run: both requests stayed on api.openai.com and were never offered to Router; the scanner reports them as 'hard limit: audio'

items.title: Summarise long chats with a cheaper model
items.summary: The history summary moves from the chat model to SUMMARY_MODEL, gpt-4o-mini by default.
items.gains: -93% on every summary in a 6-conversation sample through Router ($0.00764 on gpt-4o against $0.00050 on gpt-4o-mini)
items.loses: A different model writes the summary, so answers will differ: the wording changed in all 6 samples while the facts were kept. It was also slower on this sample, mean 1487 ms against 1161 ms, because gpt-4o-mini writes a few more output tokens; a user waits for this call, but only on the turns where the history overflows.
items.why: __summarise compresses a conversation into 700 characters or less, a short and fully specified job, and it was using whatever OPENAI_MODEL is set to. The new SUMMARY_MODEL setting defaults to gpt-4o-mini and is documented in README.md and .env.example; setting it to the same value as OPENAI_MODEL restores the old behaviour, and the code falls back to OPENAI_MODEL when the key is absent, so an OpenAIHelper built from another config is unaffected.

evidence.detail: 6 sample conversations summarised through both models via Router (12 of 12 requests 200): totals $0.00764 on gpt-4o against $0.00050 on gpt-4o-mini, mean latency 1161 ms against 1487 ms; both summaries of each conversation kept the same facts in different words
the repo's suite with Router on: 5 passed; tests/test_function_call_history.py: 3 passed

items.title: Three Router levers left alone and why
items.summary: Fallbacks, a provider timeout and a prompt cache key were considered for these calls and not taken.
items.why: Router fallbacks could replace the tenacity retry on RateLimitError, which currently makes a user wait 20 s a time for up to three attempts, but a fallback candidate answers silently with a different model and the response gives no sign of it: that is a product call about whether a Telegram user may get an answer from another vendor, not a migration detail. A provider_timeout would cap how long a user can wait on a stalled provider (the SDK's own default is 600 s), but it introduces a plain-text 504 path that the bot would show as a generic error, and there is no measurement here of how often that would fire. prompt_cache_key pays only above a 1,024-token identical prefix; this bot's fixed prefix is a one-line assistant prompt and the rest of the history differs per chat, so a per-feature key would buy provider affinity and little else. Each of the three is a one-line addition to router.policy.json if the reviewer wants it.

evidence.detail: catalog cache_read for gpt-4o is $1.25 per 1M against $2.50 input, so caching would halve the input cost of a cached prefix if one existed above the 1,024-token minimum
